meta.pageTitle: Bible Study — September 29 | Follow Jesus Your Own Way
meta.title: Follow Jesus Your Own Way:
meta.footer: Bible Study — September 29  ·  Ordinary Glory: Follow Jesus Your Own Way  ·  Scripture from the NIV

summary.speaker: Pastor Chris
summary.bigIdea: Follow Jesus in your own way. Be fully yourself, and let God’s love be seen through your life.
summary.overview: Chris tells how his daughter explained why he loves his work. He says the world needs Christians who are real, not a stereotype, and he gives four points about what that looks like.

points.title: Be Fully You
points.text: No one else has your gifts, humor, or personality. When you live with hope as the person God made you to be, people notice and ask about it. Look at your own life before you judge others.

points.title: Grace Over Judgment
points.text: Let Jesus define what a Christian is, not the loudest voices. Jesus says we know people by their fruit, which means how they live and how they treat others.

points.title: Blessed to Be a Blessing
points.text: We are blessed so that we can bless others, even a server who is having a hard day. Jesus says people will know us by our love, especially for those who are often left out.

points.title: Broken Vessels, Bold Reconciliation
points.text: You do not need to be perfect for God to use you, because God’s power shows in weakness. We have been reconciled to God, and we are asked to help others come back to God and to each other.

summary.takeaway: Think of someone who showed you God’s love, and ask how you can be that kind of person for someone else this week.

pet3.text: “But in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who speak maliciously against your good behavior in Christ may be ashamed of their slander.”

matt7.text: “Watch out for false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ferocious wolves. By their fruit you will recognize them. Do people pick grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? Likewise, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus, by their fruit you will recognize them.”

john13.text: “A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.”

john4.text: “No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is made complete in us.”

matt25.text: “Then the King will say to those on his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father; take your inheritance, the kingdom prepared for you since the creation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in, I needed clothes and you clothed me, I was sick and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to visit me.’ Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you something to drink? When did we see you a stranger and invite you in, or needing clothes and clothe you? When did we see you sick or in prison and go to visit you?’ The King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.’”

cor4.text: “But we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this all-surpassing power is from God and not from us.”

cor12.text: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on me.”

cor5.text: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting people’s sins against them. And he has committed to us the message of reconciliation. We are therefore Christ’s ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us. We implore you on Christ’s behalf: Be reconciled to God.”

questions.text: Pastor Chris said he sometimes wants a t-shirt that says, “I’m a Dolly Parton kind of Christian” — a little bit of a mess, but full of real, vibrant faith. He also said he wants to be a “Fred Rogers kind of Christian,” the kind who tells people they matter, echoing Fred Rogers’s own words: “I like you just the way you are.” In Hamlet, Shakespeare has a flawed father tell his son, “This above all: to thine own self be true.” Pastor Chris said the invitation is to stop comparing yourself to some version of who you think you were supposed to be, and just start being fully you — the good, the bad, and the ugly. Think of a “kind of Christian” description you could honestly give yourself, based on your real personality and story, not a Sunday-best version of you. What is one part of the real, unpolished you that you have been hiding from your small group or church family, and what would it take for you to bring that part into the light?

Pastor Chris’s main point today was simple: “Follow Jesus your own way. Nobody else is like you. Nobody else has the gifts or talents that you have.” Peter writes that when we live with real hope, we should “always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have” (1 Peter 3:15–16), because people notice hope that does not fall apart under pressure. Pastor Chris gave examples: staying hopeful while your kid is in a mental health crisis, or trusting God is up to something good after losing a job. Think of a hard season you are in right now, or one you have already lived through — something at work, at home, or with your health. What would it actually look like for you, with your own personality and gifts, to live through that season in a way that makes people curious enough to ask you why you still have hope?

Pastor Chris remembered riding loose in the back of a pickup truck as a kid — something every parent did back then without a second thought, but something that would get you arrested today. He said, “Most Christians are professionals at contemplating the sins of other people,” and that we love playing morality police instead of dealing with our own struggles. He asked instead, “How do I live as faithfully as I can today? How do I live as lovingly as I can today?” Think of something from your own past — a choice, a habit, a belief — that felt completely normal at the time but that you, or the world, now sees very differently. How does remembering that change the way you judge other people’s choices today, especially the choices you feel most tempted to criticize?

Pastor Chris warned that any version of Christianity with an adjective in front of it — “Christian nationalist,” “progressive Christian” — is really something else wearing Jesus as a costume. Jesus himself warned that false prophets “come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ferocious wolves,” and that “by their fruit you will recognize them” (Matthew 7:15–20). Pastor Chris said the real test is simple: go to a restaurant with someone and watch how they treat the server. Think of a person whose politics, denomination, or label made you unsure about them, but whose actual behavior toward others convinced you they were the real thing — or convinced you they were not. What label or adjective do you sometimes let define your own faith more than Jesus does, and what would it look like this week to check the actual fruit of your life instead?

At a restaurant in Waco, Pastor Chris’s waiter admitted he had struggled with addiction his whole life and had just reached six months of sobriety. Pastor Chris said in that moment, his mission was not to be served well, but to be a blessing to a vulnerable man — because, as the Bible says, we “were blessed to be a blessing.” Jesus said the world would know his followers “by this… that you love one another” (John 13:34–35), and John adds that when we love one another, “God lives in us and his love is made complete in us” (1 John 4:12) — our ordinary love is literally how an invisible God becomes visible. Think of the most forgettable, everyday place you will be this week — a checkout line, your commute, a waiting room. Who is one person you could unexpectedly bless there, and what is stopping you from actually doing it instead of just noticing them?

Jesus said that whatever we do for “the least of these” — the hungry, the stranger, the immigrant, the sick, the imprisoned — we do directly to him (Matthew 25:34–40). Pastor Chris was direct: “You don’t need a theologian… you don’t need to pray about it. You know what you do if you meet an immigrant? If you meet a foreigner, you show love and kindness and hospitality.” He also described men who almost skipped a weekend serving at a prison, only to call it the best weekend of their year. Which group in Matthew 25’s list — the stranger, the sick, the imprisoned, the poor — is hardest for you personally to welcome, and why do you think that one is harder for you than the others? What is one concrete, uncomfortable step you could take this month to show hospitality to someone in that exact group?

Paul says God’s power is deliberately carried in fragile, ordinary containers — “we have this treasure in jars of clay” (2 Corinthians 4:7) — and that God told him directly, “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Martin Luther King Jr. warned that our lives are often “characterized by a high blood pressure of creeds and an anemia of deeds” — we know a lot, but we do very little. Pastor Chris said some of us stay quiet about our faith because we think we have “messed up too much” to represent God well. What is one mistake, failure, or weakness from your own life that you have been treating like a disqualification, instead of the cracked-clay-jar way God actually plans to use you? What is one small, faithful action — a “deed,” not just a belief — you could take this week instead of waiting to feel ready?

Paul says every believer has been given “the ministry of reconciliation” — we are “Christ’s ambassadors” sent to remind people they are loved and not counted against for their sins (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote, “The church is church only when it is there for others,” and Henri Nouwen wrote that “compassion asks us to go where it hurts, to enter places of pain.” Pastor Chris described the women from his church spending a weekend at a safe house for trafficking survivors in Mexico City, doing nails and having conversations at a block party for the men and women who work the streets there — and coming home saying it was the happiest they had been all year. Where is a “place of pain” near you — in your own family, workplace, or neighborhood — that you have been avoiding because entering it looks inconvenient or uncomfortable? What would it cost you personally to become an ambassador of reconciliation there, and do you believe, like the women on that trip, it might actually become the best thing you do this year?

prayer.label: Closing Prayer
prayer.text:
Dear God,

Thank you for making us each different, with our own gifts, our own humor, and our own way of following you. Forgive us for the energy we waste comparing ourselves to who we think we’re supposed to be instead of becoming who you already made us.

Teach us to live with a hope that is visible to the people around us — in hard seasons, not just easy ones — so that our lives make people curious about you.

Free us from being professionals at noticing everyone else’s faults. Help us instead to simply ask, every day, how we can live faithfully and lovingly today.

Let Jesus, and not a label or a slogan, define what it means for us to follow him. And let the fruit of our lives — how we treat a waiter, a stranger, an immigrant, a person in need — be the truest evidence of what we believe.

Thank you that you use jars of clay, not perfect vessels, and that your power shows up clearest in our weakness. Give us the courage to act instead of only believing, and to go toward the places of pain we would rather avoid.

Remind us that we were blessed to be a blessing, and that you have made us ambassadors of reconciliation — sent to remind everyone we meet that they are loved, just as they are.

We ask this in the name of Jesus, who calls us to follow him each in our own true way. Amen.
prayer.source: — Based on this week’s study: authenticity, grace over judgment, being blessed to be a blessing, and the ministry of reconciliation.
